analogy.name: A shipping parcel
analogy.line: A box is like a parcel: the item is the content, bubble wrap is padding, the cardboard is the border, and the gap to the next parcel on the shelf is the margin.

html-css.caption: Every element is a parcel. When a layout looks wrong, one of the four layers is bigger or smaller than you assumed.
steps: Margin is the shelf space around the parcel. It pushes neighbours away, and two vertical margins can merge into one, which surprises people.
Border is the cardboard. Its width counts toward the box size unless you set box-sizing: border-box. Interviewers love this one.
Padding is the bubble wrap between the cardboard and the item. It sits inside the border and takes the element's background.
Content is the item itself, the text and images. The width you set targets this part, and padding and border add on top by default.

analogy.name: A company org chart
analogy.line: State is like a manager who holds the budget: orders go down the chain as props, and requests for change travel back up as events.

react.caption: Data flows down, events flow up. That single direction is why a React tree is easy to reason about.
steps: The manager (App) owns the data. Real name: the component holding the state. Children never own it, they only receive it.
The Header is a team member handed a task sheet. Real name: a component reading props. It renders what it is given and cannot change it.
Main is a team member who files a request instead of editing the budget. It raises an event and the parent changes the state, a classic interview point.
The Footer gets the same sheet, so it shows the same thing. Real name: a pure render from props, same input and same output.

analogy.name: A security guard on rounds
analogy.line: Change detection is like a guard walking rounds after every alarm: he checks each door against his list and only fixes the ones that changed. OnPush tells him to skip rooms.

angular.caption: Angular does not watch your data. After something happens it re-checks bindings, and OnPush lets a component say it needs no check.
steps: The alarm goes off. Real name: an event such as a click, a timer or an HTTP response. Something happened, so something may have changed.
The control room hears the alarm end. Real name: Zone.js, which tells Angular the task finished and the app may be different now.
The guard compares each door with his list. Real name: every binding is checked, old value against new. OnPush components skip this walk.
The guard fixes only the changed doors. Real name: only the changed bindings are written to the DOM, which is why this is fast enough.

analogy.name: A pizza kitchen order
analogy.line: The rendering path is like making a pizza: dough (HTML), toppings plan (CSS), the assembled order (render tree), laying it out on the tray (layout), then the oven (paint).

browser-performance.caption: Five steps stand between your HTML and a pixel. Anything blocking the first two delays everything after it.
steps: HTML is the dough being shaped. Real name: the DOM, built tag by tag as the browser parses. Slow or blocked parsing delays the whole meal.
CSS is the toppings plan. Real name: the CSSOM. The browser will not serve an unstyled pizza, so CSS blocks rendering. Say that in interviews.
The render tree is the finished order slip: dough plus toppings, minus anything not on the menu. Hidden elements are left out.
Layout is placing every pizza on the tray with an exact size and spot. A change to one width can force the whole tray to be redone, called reflow.
Paint is the oven: pixels finally appear. Repaints are cheap, but a reflow sends you back to layout first and costs far more.

analogy.name: A building for everyone
analogy.line: POUR is like four rules for a public building: signs people can see or hear, doors anyone can open, clear layouts, and wiring that survives renovations.

accessibility.caption: If any one of the four promises fails, a group of users is locked out, so the page is not accessible.
steps: Perceivable is signs in big print and braille. Real name: text alternatives, contrast and captions, so everyone can sense the content.
Operable is doors anyone can open. Real name: everything works by keyboard, with enough time and no focus traps. Test it by unplugging the mouse.
Understandable is a clear floor plan. Real name: readable language and predictable behavior, with helpful messages when input goes wrong.
Robust is wiring that survives renovations. Real name: valid, semantic markup that assistive tech can parse today and after the next browser update.

analogy.name: A library with a reading desk
analogy.line: Server state is like library books on your desk: the real copy lives on the shelf, your copy can go out of date, and a librarian (the cache) knows when to fetch a fresh one.

state-management.caption: Server state lives elsewhere and goes stale, so it needs a keyed cache. That is the job React Query and SWR do.
steps: You ask for a book by its catalog number. Real name: the component requests data by a query key, such as ['todos', id].
The librarian checks your desk first. Real name: the cache. If the book is fresh it is handed over instantly with no network call.
A stale or missing book is fetched from the shelf while you keep reading the old copy. Real name: a background refetch, so the screen never blanks.
The new copy replaces the old one and the page updates. Real name: cache update and re-render, with no hand-written loading state for known data.
